paras: The attempted lynching of Dan Hinds took place on the afternoon of June 5, 1903, at a button factory in Madison, Indiana, where young men employed at the factory seized Hinds, an 18-year-old Black man, put a rope around his neck and threatened to hang him. They accused him of attempting to assault a white girl who worked there, but held him until the sheriff arrested him, and he was kept for the grand jury. A brief wire account circulated nationally, and two papers printed it as an instance of "mob law".

According to a special dispatch to the Indianapolis Journal, Hinds had lately been employed on the steamer City of Wheeling. The wire version named the workplace as Melish's button factory and the girl as Humphreys.

The Journal's correspondent wrote that Hinds "invaded the premises" of the factory that afternoon and "is alleged to have attempted to assault" a white girl employee. Young men of the factory caught him and threw a rope around his neck. In the Journal's account they "threatened to hang him, but only held him" until Sheriff Crozier arrived and arrested him. The wire report said only that the sheriff "secured the prisoner, however," and held him for a grand jury investigation.

The Journal predicted that the grand jury then in session would indict Hinds. No report of an indictment, a trial or Hinds's later fate appears in the coverage, and none mentions any action against the men who seized him.

Only the Indianapolis Journal carried a dispatch from Madison, headed "Alleged Attempt to Assnult [Assault]," which treated the charge as an allegation. The wire paragraph, which ran in the Minneapolis Journal on June 6 and then in country weeklies in Wisconsin, North Dakota, South Dakota and Minnesota through June 20, stated the attempted assault as fact and appeared among unrelated crime items. The Rock Island Argus on June 8 placed it under the subhead "Mob Law We Have Always With Us," beside the jail lynching and burning of W. T. Wyatt at Belleville, Illinois, and the Plymouth Tribune, an Indiana weekly, ran it under the same heading on June 11.
Every report found ran in white papers, from the Indianapolis Journal's dispatch to the wire roundups; no coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Dan Hinds
bases: Young men at a button factory seized Dan Hinds, put a rope around his neck and threatened to hang him over an alleged attempted assault, until the sheriff took him (A2, A3).

Hinds was not killed; the factory men seized him without authority and threatened to hang him for an alleged assault, but they held him for the sheriff, who arrested him (A2, A3). This was a threatened or attempted lynching; the number of men is not given.
The Indianapolis Journal's special dispatch (A2) and the separately worded wire brief (A3, A4) agree on the seizure, the rope, the accusation and the sheriff's intervention.

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Journal headed its dispatch 'Alleged Attempt to Assnult [Assault]' and called the accusation alleged while stating the grand jury 'will indict him'.
Most papers ran the wire brief in roundups, stating the attempted assault as fact ('for an attempted assault').
The Rock Island Argus ran the brief under 'Mob Law We Have Always With Us', next to the Belleville burning of W. T. Wyatt; the Plymouth Tribune used the same heading.
